content:
Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award winner who was this offseason's most coveted free agent, has agreed a nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets, according to multiple reports on Sunday. ESPN's Jeff Passan first reported the terms of the deal, which a person familiar with the negotiations confirmed to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because the agreement is subject to Skubal passing a physical. The contract is the largest ever given to a pitcher in Major League Baseball history, shattering the previous record by $125 million.

The numbers behind the deal are staggering. At $50 million a year, Skubal's average annual value is the highest ever for a pitcher, comfortably ahead of the $43.33 million a year the Mets previously paid Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander. The $450 million total eclipses Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million, 12-year contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers, signed before the 2024 season. Among all players, only three deals are bigger: Juan Soto's $765 million, Shohei Ohtani's $700 million and Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s $500 million. According to reports, the agreement includes a full no-trade clause, no opt-out clauses and no option years, $30 million in deferred payments from 2036 to 2045, and a $45 million signing bonus.

The timing of the deal is no accident, and it reveals one of its most carefully negotiated features. The agreement was struck just over a week before a potential lockout that is expected to begin on December 1 and shutter all offseason activity. According to a person familiar with the negotiations who spoke to The Associated Press, the $45 million signing bonus is structured so that it is shielded from the lockout that threatens the 2027 season, meaning Skubal will be paid even if baseball's labour dispute freezes the sport. For a player entering free agency at the top of the market, securing money that cannot be held hostage by a work stoppage was a priority, and it helps explain why both sides moved quickly to complete the deal before the deadline.

For the Mets, the record price buys the best pitcher in baseball and an answer to a rotation that badly needs one. New York's starters ranked 23rd in the majors in ERA at 4.47 last season, 22nd in WHIP at 1.33 and just 26th in wins, and the club endured its first last-place finish in the National League East since 2003. Skubal, by contrast, has been the most dependable and dominant starter in the game over the last three seasons. He won the American League Cy Young Award in 2024 and 2025 with the Detroit Tigers, winning 31 games with a 2.30 ERA across those two seasons, and he has posted a sub-1.00 WHIP in each of his last four seasons. Split between Detroit and the Dodgers last season after an August trade, he went 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA, a 0.96 WHIP and 186 strikeouts against just 27 walks in 158 2/3 innings, despite missing six weeks following elbow surgery. For his career, he owns a 66-44 record with a 3.02 ERA and 1,075 strikeouts in 925 1/3 innings.

The deal also cements the Mets as baseball's most extravagant spenders. As The Athletic's Jayson Stark noted, the Mets now employ the highest-paid position player and the highest-paid pitcher in the sport: Soto and Skubal will cost the club a combined $907.3 million over the next nine seasons. Owner Steve Cohen has now landed the biggest player on the market in two of the last three offseasons, and the Skubal signing follows the same pattern as the Soto deal, with the Mets simply outbidding every rival for the player they wanted most. According to The Athletic, the Toronto Blue Jays did make a serious attempt, offering Skubal a nine-year deal of their own, but the offer was not close to the $450 million the Mets ultimately paid.

Yet the record contract also carries real risk, and the Mets have accepted it without an escape hatch. Skubal is 30 years old and has undergone three surgeries on his left arm in his career, including an experimental, minimally invasive procedure in May that removed loose bodies from his elbow using NanoScope technology. That procedure allowed him to return faster than is typical, but he still missed six weeks of the season. With no opt-outs and a full no-trade clause, there is a strong likelihood that Skubal will end his career with the Mets, which means the club is betting that his arm will hold up not just in 2027 but over the full lifetime of the most lucrative deal ever given to a pitcher. Since 2023, when Skubal elevated from promising starter to bona fide star, there has not been a better pitcher in the majors, with a 2.47 ERA and 10.88 strikeouts per nine innings married to rare command of just 1.57 walks per nine, but nine years is a long time for any arm, let alone one with his surgical history.

If the physical goes as expected, the Mets will formally announce the signing in the coming days, and Skubal will be presented as the ace of a rotation the club hopes can carry it back to the playoffs. He was not simply the best pitcher on the market; as analysts have noted, he was the best pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole after the 2019 season. The Mets paid a record price to make sure he did not go anywhere else, and they did it before the lockout clock ran out. summary: Two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal has agreed a nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets, the largest deal ever given to a pitcher, according to reports on Sunday.
title: Tarik Skubal Agrees Record $450 Million Deal With New York Mets
